quote: A sufficiently young child, or a sufficiently ancient Greek philosopher, would not know that there were such things as “acoustic vibrations” or “auditory experiences.” There would just be a single thing that happened when a tree fell; a single event called “sound.”
content: The ancient Greek philosopher knew. Aristotle's De Anima II.8 (419b–420b, no DOI) distinguishes sound as a motion of air produced by the impact of solid bodies from hearing as the reception of that motion in the ear, and discusses whether a sounding body and the medium can exist without a hearer. The Stoics defined sound as struck air; Vitruvius (De Architectura V.3) compared sound to ripples on water. The distinction the essay presents as 'a big, difficult scientific challenge' that the ancients could not have made was a commonplace of ancient natural philosophy, in the very author the sequence has been using as its foil for classical categories.

quote: Every now and then one sees a press release claiming that a research study has “explained consciousness” because a team of neurologists investigated a 40Hz electrical rhythm
content: The 40 Hz proposal is Crick and Koch's (Seminars in the Neurosciences 2, 1990, no DOI), and its authors were explicit that they were proposing a neural correlate, not an explanation, and that the hard problem was being set aside. The distinction the essay goes on to draw, between access, self-awareness, wakefulness and phenomenal experience, is Block's access/phenomenal distinction (Block 1995) with Rosenthal's higher-order theories for reflectivity. The essay's press-release strawman is not the field; the field made the essay's distinction first and in more detail.

quote: But what this feels like from inside is not so much zooming in on a map, as fissioning an indivisible atom—taking one thing (it felt like one thing) and splitting it into two or more things.
content: The process has a name and a literature: conceptual differentiation. Wiser and Carey traced how the seventeenth-century Experimenters ran heat and temperature together in a single concept and how the split was achieved (Wiser & Carey, in Mental Models, 1983, no DOI), and Carey's The Origin of Concepts (2009, no DOI) treats differentiation and coalescence as the basic operations of conceptual change in both children and the history of science. This annotation is a positive one: the essay's picture is correct, and the reader who wants to see it studied rather than illustrated with a detective story has somewhere to go.
